answer_text:
Let

\[
F(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds.
\]

Since \(f\) is continuous and non-negative, \(F\) is differentiable, \(F(0)=0\), \(F(t)\ge 0\), and

\[
F'(t)=f(t).
\]

The given condition becomes

\[
F'(t)\le F(t)\qquad (0\le t\le 1).
\]

Now define

\[
G(t)=e^{-t}F(t).
\]

Then

\[
G'(t)=e^{-t}(F'(t)-F(t))\le 0.
\]

Thus \(G\) is non-increasing on \([0,1]\). Since \(F(0)=0\), we have

\[
G(0)=e^0F(0)=0.
\]

Therefore, for every \(t\in[0,1]\),

\[
G(t)\le G(0)=0.
\]

But \(F(t)\ge 0\) and \(e^{-t}>0\), so

\[
G(t)=e^{-t}F(t)\ge 0.
\]

Hence

\[
G(t)=0
\]

for all \(t\in[0,1]\). Therefore \(F(t)=0\) for all \(t\in[0,1]\), and since \(f(t)=F'(t)\), we get

\[
f(t)=0
\]

for all \(t\in[0,1]\).

Conversely, the zero function clearly satisfies the inequality. Thus the only solution is

\[
\boxed{f(t)\equiv 0\ \text{on }[0,1]}.
\]
